title: Subscription Management Platform
body: Three services — identity, tenant management, and billing — each with its own database (MySQL, MongoDB, Postgres), behind a React SPA. This repo is the orchestrator: the services live in separate repos, wired in as Git submodules, and docker compose up boots all three plus their databases with seeded schemas.

Each service is layered domain → application → infrastructure → presentation, and the two SQL services skip an ORM in favor of a hand-rolled QueryBuilder and TransactionManager — joins, pagination, and transaction boundaries are explicit instead of inferred.

Multi-tenancy works by re-issuing the JWT when a user switches organizations, rather than trusting a header on each request — the token itself carries which org you're acting as and what you're allowed to do there.

Creating a company synchronously calls the billing service over HTTP to provision its subscription. That's a real coupling point: if the call fails, the company still exists without a subscription — there's no saga or compensating transaction. That's the first thing I'd add if this needed to hold up past a portfolio piece.

Recurring billing runs outside the request path, on two Lambdas over daily EventBridge schedules. Renewal processes one subscription per transaction so a bad row doesn't block the batch; expiration is a single set-based UPDATE since it doesn't need per-row logic. Feature entitlements are their own endpoint, so other services can check quota without embedding billing logic.

title: Distributed Microservices System
body: Six repos: an API gateway in front of auth, products, orders, and payments services, with NATS handling async communication between them. Stripe is integrated in payments.

The part worth pointing at — each service uses a different datastore on purpose. Postgres for orders, MongoDB for auth, SQLite for products, all behind Prisma. Not because a system this size needs three databases, but because I wanted to work through what per-service persistence actually costs you: migrations, local dev setup, and the fact that you give up joins across service boundaries whether you planned for it or not.
The whole stack comes up with one docker compose up. Built independently.

title: Iglua Órdenes — field service management
body: The product I work on at Iglua: service orders, technician dispatch, and support tickets for companies running field operations. Five core services on a hybrid SQL/NoSQL split — MySQL where orders need relational integrity, MongoDB where client-defined report templates need to stay schemaless.

My work here is covered in more detail under Experience — the Hono reporting engine that replaced a paper process, the Kubernetes memory fix, and the centralized query engine. Listed here because it's the system most of my production time goes into, not as a separate project.
